summary:
Oregon is among the more protective United States jurisdictions for a trans visitor at state level. A July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, built from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, places Oregon in a fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington. The same ranking records that the worst-law states carry up to five-year prison terms for gender-identity-based offences or arrest policies for bathroom use, a contrast that frames Oregon's position.

Statewide anti-discrimination protection has been in force since 1 January 2008 under the Oregon Equality Act, signed 9 May 2007, which prohibits unfair discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations on the basis of gender identity. The statute defines sexual orientation to include gender identity regardless of whether identity, appearance, expression or behaviour differs from that traditionally associated with sex assigned at birth. Senate Bill 2, signed by Governor Ted Kulongoski on 9 May 2007, extended the same prohibition across employment, housing, public accommodation, public education and public services, with exemptions for religious employers, organizations and institutions, creating uniform statewide protections that do not depend on locality. An October 2019 executive order added gender identity to a 1987 policy barring state agencies from unlawful discrimination and required a third gender option, X; June 2021 legislation updated the 2008 definition of gender identity, effective immediately.

State hate-crime statutes provide additional penalties for crimes motivated by the victim's gender identity. Senate Bill 704, signed in May 2021 and effective 1 January 2022, abolished the gay panic and trans panic defences in murder, manslaughter and hate-crime cases.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Since 2014 sex reassignment surgery has not been required to change the gender marker on an Oregon birth certificate solely by request. A 10 June 2016 circuit court ruling allowed a resident to legally change gender to non-binary, which the Transgender Law Center believed was the first such ruling in the United States. Since 1 July 2017 the Department of Motor Vehicles has offered an X marker designating neutral or non-binary identity on licences and IDs, and X is also available on birth certificates. May 2017 legislation abolished the 1991 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before a legal change of sex.

Oregon operates a healthcare shield law. The MAP Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, data as of 27 September 2026, lists Oregon as a state with a shield law or executive order from 2023. The shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is legal in Oregon has been banned in the patient's home state, which is directly relevant to visitors travelling from ban states. The law was signed by Governor Tina Kotek on 13 July 2023 after passing the House in May 2023 and, following a Republican boycott, passing the Senate with watered-down amendments. Nationally the same source records 16 states and the District of Columbia holding shields, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, while 32 states and 5 territories, 56%, hold none.

Public funding for gender-affirming care is established in Oregon. In January 2013, as part of a discrimination settlement, the state agreed to provide full medical insurance coverage for gender-affirming surgeries, drugs and related treatments on public employee health plans. In August 2014 officials announced Medicaid would begin covering gender-affirming hormone therapy and other gender-affirming healthcare.

Trans-inclusive school policy has survived litigation. A transgender-inclusive public schools policy withstood challenge after the District Court ruled against plaintiffs on 24 July 2018, the Ninth Circuit upheld it on 12 February 2020, and the Supreme Court denied certiorari in December 2020 in Parents for Privacy v. Barr. April 2019 legislation, signed 6 May, amended a 1951 mental health law that had equated transvestites with pedophilia, passing 58-2 in the House and 29-0 in the Senate.

Two 2025 federal actions cut against this record. In July 2025 the Ninth Circuit ruled Oregon's adoption requirement to respect, accept and support a child's gender expression and sexual orientation unconstitutional, after the Department of Human Services prevented a woman from adopting. In June 2025 the United States Department of Education announced a Title IX investigation into the Oregon Department of Education for allowing transgender women to compete in women's sports.

Marriage and partnership recognition is settled state law. Same-sex marriage was legalized on 19 May 2014 when Judge Michael McShane struck down the 2004 Ballot Measure 36 constitutional amendment under the Equal Protection Clause; marriages from other jurisdictions have been recognized since 16 October 2013 per a Department of Justice opinion, and gender-neutral marriage was codified effective 1 January 2016. Domestic partnerships have been available since 4 February 2008 under the Family Fairness Act, and benefits to same-sex partners of state employees have been provided since 1998. Oregon decriminalized same-sex sexual activity in 1972 following the 1971 repeal of the consensual sodomy law, with an age of consent of 18; a lewd solicitation provision was struck down on free speech grounds in a unanimous 1981 Oregon Supreme Court decision. Oregon became the third state to ban conversion therapy on minors, signed by Governor Kate Brown on 18 May 2015 and effective 1 July 2015. The state anti-bullying law covers bullying, cyberbullying and harassment in all public schools on the basis of sexual orientation among other categories. Same-sex couples, married or unmarried, may apply to adopt; lesbian couples have access to assisted reproduction including in vitro fertilization, with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized as legal parent if married; surrogacy is neither expressly prohibited nor permitted, though courts are generally favourable including for same-sex couples.
tangentialFactors:
Oregon's protective posture sits within a national landscape where the same conduct can be criminal elsewhere. The July 2026 ranking records that the worst-law states carry up to five-year prison terms, with Idaho named, and arrest policies for gender-identity bathroom use, with Florida named. A visitor moving between states should not assume Oregon's rules travel with them.

The shield law's value depends on where the visitor is coming from. MAP records that 32 states and 5 territories, 56% of the national picture, hold no shield, and that youth-care bans are tracked nationally with some permanently blocked. A visitor from a ban state is the person the Oregon shield is written for.

Two federal actions in 2025 bear on Oregon's own institutions rather than on visitors directly: the Ninth Circuit's July 2025 ruling against Oregon's adoption requirement, and the June 2025 Department of Education Title IX investigation into the Oregon Department of Education over transgender women in women's sports. Both indicate that state-level protection in Oregon is being tested by federal litigation and enforcement.
